opening.say: Take any right triangle, the kind with one perfectly square corner, and call its two short sides a and b.
The long side, sitting across from the square corner, we'll call c. It's always the longest one of the three.
Pythagoras claimed these three lengths are locked together by one tidy rule, and the proof is really about area.

more.say: Try a concrete one: legs of three and four. Guess how long the slanted side has to be.
Squares on those legs have areas nine and sixteen. Add them and you get twenty-five.
And twenty-five is exactly five squared, so the slanted side is five. That's no accident.

plan.setup: Watch what happens to the squares on each side.
plan.narration: [[square-big]]Here's a big square, side a plus b. [[four-triangles]]Tuck four copies of our triangle inside, one in each corner. [[tilted-square]]What's left is a tilted square with side c. [[rearrange]]Now slide the triangles into two corners instead. [[two-squares]]The leftover space becomes a squared plus b squared. Same area, so it equals c squared.
plan.plan:
square-big: a large square with side a plus b appears, each side split into a segment of length a and a segment of length b.
four-triangles: four identical right triangles with legs a and b appear in the corners, hypotenuses facing inward.
tilted-square: the middle gap highlights as a tilted square whose side is c, so its area is c squared.
rearrange: the triangles slide so two rectangles of a by b form, leaving the same total uncovered area.
two-squares: the leftover region shows a square of area a squared and a square of area b squared, labeled equal to c squared.
plan.close: Would the same trick work if the corner weren't square?
